title: A covenant (CCC 1601; 1644)
hook: marriage as a lifelong covenant of partners

segments.voice: Yesterday, celibacy, and the married priests of the Eastern Churches. Your line was two traditions. Today, a new week, and from the priesthood to marriage. Day one thousand one hundred seven.

A phone contract has a term. A lease has an end date. A gym membership, until you finally find the cancel button. Contracts are useful. They say what each side owes, for how long, and what happens if someone doesn't deliver. Then, on a Saturday afternoon, two people stand at the front of a church and promise something with no end date, no exit clause, and no list of deliverables: for better, for worse, in sickness and in health. Whatever that is, it's not a phone plan. The Catechism has a name for it, an old word with deep roots in the Bible, and it's today's word.
screen: `A TERM. AN END DATE.` → `NO END DATE.` → `NOT A PHONE PLAN.`

segments.voice: The Catechism opens its teaching on marriage with this word: covenant. It describes marriage as a covenant by which a man and a woman form between themselves a partnership of the whole of life, ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children. And it says that between the baptized, Christ raised this covenant to the dignity of a sacrament. What makes a covenant different? Some teachers put it this way. A contract trades things: money for a service, rent for a room. A covenant gives persons. In a contract you say, I'll do this if you do that. In a covenant you say, I am yours. Covenants run through the Bible. God makes them with Noah, with Abraham, with Israel at Sinai, and the prophets keep reaching for marriage to describe them: God as a faithful husband who doesn't walk away, even when his people do. So when the Church calls marriage a covenant, it's borrowing the language God uses about his own faithfulness. In Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wherefore a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they shall be two in one flesh." Then the Catechism draws out what follows. The love of the spouses, it says, by its very nature asks for unity and indissolubility: a partnership meant to last the whole of life. And it asks for faithfulness. The Catechism roots this in God's own fidelity and in Christ's love for the Church. That's why a Catholic wedding has vows, not terms. The couple gives consent, freely, in front of witnesses. And in the Latin Church, Catholic teaching says the couple themselves are the ministers of the sacrament: the priest or deacon witnesses, but the two of them give it to each other.
screen: `A PARTNERSHIP OF THE WHOLE OF LIFE.` · `A CONTRACT TRADES THINGS. A COVENANT GIVES PERSONS.` · `TWO IN ONE FLESH.` · `UNITY, FAITHFULNESS, FOR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a couple in trouble. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one couple who are struggling right now. Maybe you know the details, maybe you just know the silence at dinner, or the way one of them talks about the other. Don't take sides. Don't try to fix it. Just hold the two of them together in your mind, side by side. If you pray, you can ask God to strengthen what they promised each other. If you don't, simply wish them patience and honest words. The bell holds the time.
A covenant. Not a trade of things, but a gift of persons: in Catholic teaching, marriage is a partnership of the whole of life, faithful and for life, raised by Christ to a sacrament. Today's word.
Your line: covenant, not contract. Today, notice one place where you keep score in a close relationship, and for one day, let the score go. Day one thousand one hundred seven.

howItsDone: At a Catholic wedding the bride and groom freely exchange their consent and vows before a priest or deacon and witnesses, and the Church regards the couple themselves as the ministers of the sacrament.

notes: CCC 1601 and 1644 paraphrased (copyrighted translation; 1601 itself quotes the Code of Canon Law, can. 1055).
Confirm Challoner wording of Genesis 2:24 exactly as quoted.
'For better, for worse, in sickness and in health' is a common wedding vow formula, given as an echo, not quoted from a rite; confirm it fits the Catholic rite's English.
'A contract trades things, a covenant gives persons' is a common catechetical contrast, not the Catechism's wording.
'The couple themselves are the ministers of the sacrament' reflects Latin-Church teaching (CCC 1623); Eastern Churches see the priest as minister of the crowning. Keeper may add that difference.
Prophets' marriage imagery (Hosea 2 and others) summarized; confirm.
Editor: the contract/covenant contrast is now attributed to 'some teachers' (not the Catechism's wording); 'the Bible is full of covenants' changed to 'covenants run through the Bible'.

Audit (2026-10-02): the teach's 'roots faithfulness in God's own fidelity and Christ's love for the Church' comes from CCC 1646–1647, outside the cited 1601/1644; added that source. Genesis 2:24 Douay wording checked.
